title: Metabolic Imaging Core
text: METABOLIC IMAGING CORE The mission of the Metabolic Imaging Core (MIC) and its three Sub-Cores (Advanced Body Composition, Positron Emission Tomography [PET], and Functional Neuroimaging) is to support nutrition and obesity research from NORC members, by providing access to advanced non-invasive imaging technologies. Since the last funding period, the MIC has enabled highly sophisticated assessments of body composition, tissue physiology and brain function that accelerated translational research in human obesity and nutrition. The NORC Metabolic Imaging Core coordinates and centralizes research imaging needs of NORC members and encourages use of advanced metabolic imaging techniques, also providing support in research design and consultation. The Advanced Body Composition Sub-Core provides services in multi-organ MRI/MR spectroscopy, CT imaging and high-throughput image analysis used in a variety of body composition assessments. The PET Sub-Core includes services of PET/CT, PET/MRI, and development of physiologic and functional radiotracers. The Functional Neuroimaging Sub-Core provides services in fMRI and structural brain imaging. The NORC combines the expertise of long-standing MGH imaging Cores, and over the last funding cycle the MIC was rated very highly by NORC members and exceptionally productive, performing over 2,000 imaging services for members, including consultation and technical support, showing sustained demand serving over 37 researchers, including 34 NORC members. The MIC also has expanded its imaging services and technological innovations, making them available to NORC investigators. The aims of the current renewal application are to: 1) Provide a variety of advanced imaging services, paired with consultation, to support studies in need of imaging-based endpoints, with continued innovation in imaging technologies, provision of new services, and expansion of user base, 2) Provide standalone imaging analysis services, including quantitative interpretation of imaging data and high-throughput body composition analyses of large datasets using deep learning algorithms developed in- house during the current funding cycle, 3) Harmonize imaging protocols used for brain, liver, muscle, and visceral fat MR studies across multiple NORCs, targeting high repeatability of MR-based measurements across Centers.

title: Impact of sex, flow, and glomerular permeability on endocytic uptake along the kidney proximal tubule
text:
Proteinuria occurs when the kidney proximal tubule is unable to fully reclaim albumin and other proteins that escape the
glomerular ﬁltration barrier, and it is linked to increased risk and progression of chronic kidney disease. This project aims
to develop a multiscale mathematical model of protein uptake along the length of the proximal tubule that includes the
impact of baseline sex diﬀerences and variations in glomerular ﬁltration of ﬂuid and protein. Ultimately, this work will
enhance our ability to predict kidney disease progression and response to potential therapeutics.

title: Determining the Origins of Nonclassical Class I molecules through Molecular and Functional Approaches
text:
Study of the evolution of the immune system permits an view of those characteristics of immunity that are vital
for defense in all animals, including humans, versus those features that are “primitive” or specific to particular
species. Our research in comparative immunology gives an overall view of immune molecules, such as the
major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, that are required to combat infectious diseases and cancer
and avoid autoimmunity. We have detected MHC molecules in sharks, the oldest animals with adaptive
immunity, that are likely the forerunners of their human counterparts. We will examine the structure and
function of these molecules to gain insight into their functions in humans.

title: Structural and Mechanistic Understanding of Antibody Inhibition of AAV2 Gene Therapy
text:
Adeno associated viruses (AAVs) are the most common viral vector for gene therapy, but not all people are
eligible for treatment due to pre-existing immunities to AAVs. This project will endeavor to design novel AAV2
escape variants and investigate the mechanism by which neutralizing antibodies inhibit viral transduction.
Production of a novel AAV2 escape variant will reduce the burden of genetic disorders on patients by
increasing the cohort of treatable patients, and determination of the mechanism of neutralization will inform
vector and treatment design thereby reducing costs and increasing safety.

title: New Classes of Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Imaging Probes With High-Spin Metal Complexes
text:
Developing new ways of noninvasively imaging the chemistry of the body is a grand challenge in
biomedical imaging. High-spin metal complexes may enable such imaging through the electron
analogue to conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) but have not yet been developed
for this technique. This proposal will do so, in the process creating a transformative new class of
molecular imaging probes.

title: Cancer Control Program
text: Cancer Control Program: Summary/Abstract The goal of the HDFCCC Cancer Control (CC) Program is to use a multi-disciplinary team approach to understand and intervene on the structural and social determinants of cancer, leading to improved cancer health outcomes and equity. This goal will be achieved by using intra- and inter-programmatic team science to advance understanding of these multilevel determinants and to develop, translate, and implement effective behavioral, clinical, and policy interventions that will reduce the burden of cancer in the catchment area and achieve equity in cancer health outcomes. The CC Program follows a “cells-to-society” approach interrogate the biological mechanisms underlying structural and social determinants of cancer and translate these into interventions. The CC Program has the capacity to integrate discovery, intervention, and delivery research. To do so, the program (1) identifies the causes of outcomes across the cancer continuum, with attention to diverse populations, including structural, social, policy, industrial, and environmental influences on tobacco use, physical activity, other risk factors, cancer screening, and care; (2) develops, implements, and evaluates evidence-based interventions to reduce the cancer burden and improve cancer health equity in the HDFCCC catchment area; and (3) translates knowledge into effective policies and programs to achieve equity in outcomes across the cancer continuum.

title: Clinical and functional assessment of glaucoma-associated mitochondrial gene variants to facilitate precision eye care
text:
Genetic studies involving thousands of individuals have identified many genes associated with glaucoma risk,
though this has not yet translated to personalized approaches for diagnosis, monitoring or treatment of this
common, blinding disease. This mentored clinician-scientist career development proposal will investigate the
clinical impact and underlying disease mechanisms for glaucoma-associated genes that function in the
mitochondria, the energy-producing parts of our cells. The approach is designed to help pave the way for
personalized glaucoma care for individuals whose disease is driven by mitochondrial gene variants; the
methodologies employed in this proposal can also be readily applied to other genes and pathways in the future
to lay the foundation for precision glaucoma care.

title: Genetic dependencies in KIAA1549-BRAF rearranged pediatric low-grade gliomas
text:
The most frequent genomic alteration in pediatric low-grade gliomas is a rearrangement that creates a fusion
between the oncogene BRAF and the uncharacterized protein KIAA1549. Inhibitors which block the function of
this fusion are effective but cause significant toxicity and require continuous dosing throughout childhood. The
goal of this project is to define new therapeutic targets in KIAA1549-BRAF mutant pLGGs, with a focus on
characterizing how the POMT complex regulates KIAA1549-BRAF activity.

title: Proteomics (PRO)
text: The Proteomics Shared Resource (PRO-SR) was included as a Developing SR in the previous Cancer Center Support Grant (CCSG) funding cycle. The goal of PRO-SR is to provide state-of-the-art instrumentation, technical expertise, and advanced informatics support for the application of mass spectrometry-based proteomics to wide-ranging queries including understanding the role of proteins in cancer development and progression, to identify cancer biomarkers and therapeutic targets. PRO-SR leadership and personnel, with their broad and deep knowledge of biology, informatics, and proteomics, educate and guide Rogel Cancer Center members to implement advanced proteomic technologies which have proven invaluable.

title: Mechanisms of Dendritic Cell State Regulation During Germinal Center Responses
text:
All licensed vaccines are designed to elicit pathogen-specific antibodies that prevent infection, but these
antibodies often lose effectiveness as pathogens evolve. This project aims to uncover mechanisms by which
specialized dendritic cells modulates the germinal center – the site where antibody quality improves – a key
strategy to enhance vaccine efficacy. By revealing new cellular mechanisms governing germinal center
responses, we hope to guide the design of next-generation vaccines that generate broader, longer-lasting
protection against rapidly evolving infectious agents.

title: Hemophilia Point-of-Care Monitoring Device and App
text:
Hemophilia A results from a deficiency of FVIII-activity and can result in severe bleeding. Head bleeds
can be debilitating and joint-bleeds require major medical intervention. The results of our efforts will be a
human-centered hemophilia Bluetooth-connected monitoring device, consumable, and app that will provide
accurate and easy FVIII and FVIII-like monitoring with the goals of decreasing risk of unexpected bleeding and
increasing patient care in all settings for traditional and novel therapies.

title: Arkansas Rural Community Health-Healthy Environmental Research (ARCH-HER) Study
text: We seek to support the Arkansas Rural Community Health Study (ARCH), established in 2007, which reported that over 45% of prevalent cases at baseline recruitment were early-onset breast cancer. By partnering with the Regional Campuses, this project will follow-up existing participants in ARCH targeting those residing in communities with high environmental exposures for additional biospecimen and exposure surveys, especially during key windows of susceptibility. The project will promote widespread data sharing and scientific collaborations with the goal to 1) enrich ARCH cohort maintenance and resource infrastructure, 2) collect longitudinal sample and exposure data, 3) develop and implement an interactive dashboard to promote cohort data management and sharing.

title: Molecular characterization of TDP-43's covalent modifications, oligomerization and pathogenesis
text:
Increasing research efforts have identified the presence of an abnormal protein, TDP-43, in the brains of
individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and other AD-related dementias.
However, the role of TDP-43 in neurodegeneration and cognitive decline remains unclear. Our project will
employ innovative techniques to investigate the protein’s modifications, aggregation, and clearance, providing
new insights into its role in neurodegeneration and cognitive impairment.

title: The role of mTOR dysregulation in poxvirus infection
text:
Despite the eradication of smallpox, members of the poxviridae family remain Category A Priority Pathogens
and pandemic threats while others are used as oncolytic therapeutics and vaccine vectors. With their unusual
level of self-sufficiency and cytoplasmic mode of DNA replication, mechanisms of host sensing and poxvirus
evasion strategies are highly complex, and many outstanding questions remain. This proposal explores a
unique strategy whereby poxviruses dysregulate the activity of the metabolic sensor and effector kinase,
mTOR, to counteract poorly understood aspects of innate responses to infection.

title: Investigating lipogenesis mediated resistance to cytotoxic therapy in PDAC
text:
This project is proposing to investigate targeting pancreatic cancer
tumor cell lipid production as a means to increasing the e5icacy of radiation therapy and
chemotherapy. We will use cell culture and animal experiments to examine how blocking
lipid synthesis e5ects the ability of tumor cells to independently survive cytotoxic therapy,
as well as the ability of the immune system to kill tumors following cytotoxic therapy. We
hope this will provide a basis for strategies targeting lipid synthesis to enhance the
e5ectiveness of treatments currently in use in patients.

title: Dynamics of Hippocampal Inputs in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
The treatment of Alzheimer's disease has been hampered by our limited understanding of how the molecular
pathology affects the neural activity that underlies cognition. The research proposed in this application will
assess how loss and dysfunction of a vulnerable type of neurons impairs how the hippocampus retrieves,
encodes, and consolidates information. It will further test an intervention to stimulate these neurons in order to
rescue memory, informing future treatments.

title: Text Mining and Large Language Models for AI-Driven Evidence-Based Functional Annotation of Clinical Variants
text:
Cancer is defined by an accumulation of genetic variants that drive tumor growth and metastasis. With the
ongoing development of therapies that target specific deregulated molecular pathways, it is increasingly
important to understand the connections between genetic variants and the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment
response of cancers. In this project, the ClinGen Somatic Knowledgebase and UniProt data resources will
collaborate on AI-driven data strategies, including the use of Large Language Models (LLMs), to extract
information about cancer variants from the scientific literature at large scale and make it accessible to
researchers and clinicians for precision medicine.

title: Mechanistic understanding of role of ATF2 signaling in radiation-induced esophageal cancer
text:
Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is the deadliest of all human squamous cell carcinomas, and has
a relatively low five-year survival rate. Abnormalities in stress response signaling and epithelial to mesenchymal
transition (EMT) have gained prominence as cancer promoting mechanisms. These studies will define whether
radiation-induced persistent pATF2 stress response signaling, is a key node in promoting EMT and changes in
the microenvironment that facilitate radiation-induced ESCC initiation and/or progression.

title: Advancing the clinical actionability of polygenic scores for coronary artery disease
text: Earlier identification of individuals at high risk for coronary artery disease is needed to allow for initiation of prevention strategies to reduce morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Polygenic scores, which can estimate an individual's genetic predisposition for disease early in life, have the potential to advance risk prediction beyond current methods based solely on clinical factors. This proposal seeks to combine newly available data and statistical methods to advance the actionability of polygenic scores by improving their performance across populations, making them more interpretable in the clinical setting, and identifying new uses for them in guiding preventive therapies.

title: Clonal Hematopoiesis in a Biracial Population
text:
The proposed research seeks to study the factors associated with development of clonal hematopoiesis of
indeterminate potential (CHIP), and racial disparities in associated outcomes, in order to identify individuals at
increased risk. With the availability of low cost sequencing techniques, we expect the number of individuals with
CHIP to increase in future, and, it will be important to develop appropriate strategies to manage these individuals.
Knowledge gained from the proposed study is expected to set the stage for interventions to inform management
of CHIP and decrease the risk of associated adverse outcomes such as hematologic malignancies,
cardiovascular disease and mortality.
